screens.title: Cloud Services and Providers — Focus on Google Cloud
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we move from cloud fundamentals to concrete services you will encounter on the job. You will meet the major cloud providers and then focus on Google Cloud Platform, exploring the compute, storage, and networking services that support applications at scale. We'll show actual command examples you can use in a terminal and discuss when to use each service. For an IT support specialist, the goal is practical familiarity: recognize service names, map them to common tasks like provisioning a virtual machine, choosing appropriate storage based on access patterns, and diagnosing connectivity issues. You will also learn how support workflows use the Cloud Console, the gcloud command-line tool, and simple monitoring checks. By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain why Compute Engine differs from App Engine, select an appropriate Cloud Storage class for archival data, and identify the first places to look when a hosted VM becomes slow. Think of this chapter as a short tour that gives you actionable vocabulary and examples you can use when supporting cloud-hosted systems. What service would you check first when a website is slow?

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.4 › Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Cloud Services and Providers

A focused tour of Google Cloud Platform's compute, storage, and networking offerings and the common tasks an IT support professional will perform.

In this lesson
Identify core GCP services and learn practical commands used in support workflows.
Coming up
Compute Engine VMs, App Engine, Cloud Functions, and storage choices.
Why it matters
Support professionals need to map symptoms to services and use the Console or gcloud to act quickly.
Explore Key Topics
Compute
Virtual machines, App Engine, Cloud Functions — pick based on control vs. convenience.
Storage
Object, block, and managed databases with storage classes for cost and access patterns.
Networking
VPCs, load balancing, DNS, CDN, and secure links to on-premises networks.
Concept map
GCP Services
Compute, Storage, Networking, IAM and Tools
Support Tools
Cloud Console, gcloud, gsutil, monitoring
Operational Focus
Performance, cost, access control, and troubleshooting

screens.title: What you'll be able to do
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives define the practical skills you'll build in this chapter. First, you will be able to identify the major cloud providers and name the core services each offers; this matters because support conversations often start by naming the provider and service involved. Second, you will explore compute services in Google Cloud — from virtual machines to serverless functions — and learn when a VM is the right choice versus App Engine or Cloud Functions. Third, you will understand storage options such as object storage, block storage, and managed databases, and how to pick a storage class for cost and access patterns. Finally, you will learn the networking building blocks used to connect resources and secure traffic, including VPCs, load balancing, and VPN. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual cue so you can recall which tool fits which task, and the verified competency milestone shows how to demonstrate that skill in a support scenario.

screens.title: Major cloud providers and why we focus on GCP
screens.narratorSegment: Many organizations rely on one of three dominant cloud providers: Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud Platform. Knowing at least one platform deeply gives you a working vocabulary and enables you to support systems effectively. This lesson focuses on Google Cloud Platform as our example set because it exposes clear service names and has both CLI and Console tools that match common support tasks. For support staff the important idea is not memorizing every product but mapping real incidents to the right service family — for instance, identifying that a VM performance problem likely involves Compute Engine and persistent disks, whereas a slow web request served by a managed platform might point to App Engine or Cloud Functions. A common misconception is that all cloud vendors are interchangeable; while they provide similar categories, each has different names, default behaviors, and tooling which affect how you diagnose issues. For example, support steps you take in the Console or via the CLI will look different across providers. Practice by picking one provider to reach competency: learn its Console layout, its CLI commands for common tasks, and the names of services you will encounter. That focused fluency makes troubleshooting faster and more accurate.

keyIdea.text: Support efficiency comes from focused familiarity with one provider's services, names, and tools.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.4 › Major Providers
The big three and why focus matters

AWS, Azure, and GCP offer comparable service families. As a support professional, targeted fluency on one provider accelerates diagnosis and action.

  • Map incidents to services: Identify whether a problem involves compute, storage, or networking before you act.
  • Console vs CLI: Learn where to check metrics in the Console and which CLI commands you will use to reproduce or fix issues.
  • Misconception: Providers are not identical; names and defaults differ and those differences affect troubleshooting steps.
Key Takeaway

Choose one major provider to master for faster, more accurate support work. Knowing service families is more important than memorizing every product.

Practical example

If a user reports a slow application, first ask whether it's running on a VM, a managed platform, or serverless. That maps the problem to Compute Engine, App Engine, or Cloud Functions respectively and narrows diagnostics.

Common mistake

Trying the same troubleshooting script across all providers can waste time because consoles and default metrics differ.

screens.title: Compute in GCP — Compute Engine (VMs)
screens.narratorSegment: Compute Engine provides virtual machines you control much like physical servers. In practice, you will create instances with a chosen machine type, operating system image, and boot disk. The important support skills are knowing how to provision a basic VM from the CLI, verify it appears in the Console, and read the instance's monitoring charts for C P U, disk input and output, and network. A concrete example command appears in the lesson content: using a gcloud compute instances create command to spin up a Debian VM in a named zone. After creating a VM, check its monitoring tab in the Console for C P U spikes, memory pressure, and disk latency. A common misconception is that VMs always need manual scaling; rather, you can provision autoscaling groups or use load balancing to distribute load. For diagnosis, start with simple metrics and then inspect persistent disk performance if disk input and output is high. As a support professional, practice a sequence: create the VM with the CLI, confirm in the Console, and collect monitoring data to form an initial hypothesis. That pattern gets you to a reproducible, evidence-backed troubleshooting step.

keyIdea.text: Create with gcloud, verify in the Console, and use monitoring graphs to prioritize CPU, memory, or disk issues.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.4 › Compute Engine
Compute Engine: virtual machines you manage

VMs offer granular control over OS, CPU, memory, and attached disks. Support work often starts by checking VM health and metrics.

Command example
gcloud compute instances create my-first-vm 
  --zone=us-central1-a 
  --machine-type=e2-medium 
  --image-project=debian-cloud 
  --image-family=debian-11 
  --boot-disk-size=20GB
Run that command to create a VM, then open the Console to view the instance entry and its Monitoring tab for CPU, disk, and network charts.
Support checklist
  • Confirm VM state and zone
  • Check CPU and disk I/O graphs
  • Review attached persistent disks
Common mistake

Assuming CPU is the issue without checking disk latency or network throughput can mislead your diagnosis.

Concrete scenario

A web server VM reports slow response times. Start by viewing CPU and disk I/O in Monitoring. If disk I/O is high, consider the persistent disk type and whether read/write patterns need a higher-performance disk.

Key Takeaway

Use gcloud to create reproducible VMs, then use Console monitoring to form an evidence-based hypothesis about performance.

screens.title: PaaS and serverless: App Engine vs Cloud Functions
screens.narratorSegment: Google Cloud offers managed compute where you don't manage the underlying servers. App Engine is a platform-as-a-service that lets developers deploy web applications without managing OS or scaling details. Cloud Functions is serverless for single-purpose event-driven functions. The practical difference is control versus convenience: App Engine supports web apps with automatic scaling while abstracting server management; Cloud Functions run tiny units of logic in response to events and are ideal for background tasks or lightweight APIs. A concrete example is deploying a small web app: App Engine is appropriate if you need routing, application frameworks, and automatic scaling for web traffic. Cloud Functions works well for processing uploaded files or responding to Pub/Sub messages. A common misconception is that serverless always costs less; costs depend on usage patterns and execution time. For support professionals, the key skill is recognizing the service type from a symptom — if the application entry points are functions and triggered by events, you will check function logs and event triggers; if it's App Engine, you will check version settings, instance class, and request latency. That mapping guides the next diagnostic steps.

keyIdea.text: App Engine for web applications; Cloud Functions for event-driven, single-purpose code — choose based on control, scaling, and execution model.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.4 › App Engine vs Functions
Managed platform vs serverless

App Engine runs web apps with automatic scaling and less operational overhead. Cloud Functions runs short-lived functions in response to events.

App Engine
  • Deploy web applications without server management
  • Automatic scaling based on traffic
  • Good for full web stacks
Cloud Functions
  • Event-driven execution
  • Short-lived, single-purpose functions
  • Ideal for file processing and lightweight APIs
Common misconception

Serverless is not always cheaper; cost depends on invocation frequency and execution duration. Evaluate expected usage patterns before deciding.

Concrete scenario

You need to run image resizing when users upload photos. A Cloud Function triggered by storage events is simpler and scales automatically for bursts, while App Engine would be heavier but suitable if resizing is part of a larger web application workflow.

Key Takeaway

Choose App Engine for full web apps and Cloud Functions for small, event-driven tasks. Your troubleshooting approach follows the execution model.

screens.title: Cloud Storage and object storage concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Cloud Storage is Google's object storage service for unstructured data such as images, backups, and static website assets. Objects live in named buckets and are accessed by path and permissions. Storage classes — Standard, Nearline, Coldline, and Archive — trade off cost and access frequency: Standard is for frequently accessed objects, Archive is for long-term retention with infrequent access. A practical command you will use as support staff is gsutil cp to upload a file to a bucket; this is useful when verifying backups or moving test artifacts. For example, copying a local file to a bucket simulates a user upload and lets you check permissions and lifecycle rules. A common mistake is placing rarely accessed archival data in a high-cost class; always align storage class with access patterns. As an IT support professional, you will often check bucket permissions, object metadata, and storage class in the Console or with gsutil to confirm whether access errors or cost concerns are caused by misconfigured classes or lifecycle settings. Cloud Storage and object storage concepts means use buckets and storage classes intentionally: align cost and access frequency, and verify with gsutil or the console.. In practical terms, buckets, objects, storage classes, and a gsutil example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.4 › Cloud Storage
Object storage basics

Cloud Storage holds objects in buckets with configurable storage classes and access controls. Use the Console or gsutil to manage objects and permissions.

Upload example
gsutil cp local-file.txt gs://my-unique-bucket-name/remote-file.txt

This command copies a local file into a bucket, which you can then inspect for storage class, ACLs, and metadata.

When to use

Backups, media, archives, and static website assets.

Common mistake

Using Standard class for rarely accessed archives increases cost unnecessarily.

Concrete scenario

A team needs to store months of logs. Recommend Coldline or Archive if access is rare, and show how to check and change lifecycle rules in the Console to move objects automatically.

Key Takeaway

Choose a storage class to match how often objects will be accessed. Use gsutil for scripted verification and the Console for quick checks.

screens.title: Persistent Disk and block storage
screens.narratorSegment: Persistent Disk is durable block storage you attach to Compute Engine VMs. Think of it like a virtual hard drive: it serves as a boot disk or data disk and is replicated to provide high availability. For operational support, Persistent Disk matters because disk performance can be a limiting factor for application throughput and database responsiveness. When diagnosing a slow VM, check whether the disk is a standard persistent disk or a higher-performance SSD-backed option, and look at disk input and output metrics in Monitoring. Another support scenario is replacing a boot disk or expanding disk size — these are common tasks you will perform via the Console or CLI. A common misconception is that Persistent Disks are automatically the same performance across machine types; performance characteristics depend on disk type and size. As a support professional, learn to identify attached disks in the instance details, examine their IOPS and throughput, and consider moving critical workloads to higher-performance disk types when justified by measured bottlenecks. Persistent Disk and block storage means persistent disk is the primary block storage for vms; disk type and size affect i/o performance and support decisions.. In practical terms, durable block storage attached to vms and its support implications. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.4 › Persistent Disk
Persistent Disk as a VM's virtual drive

Used for boot disks and application storage, persistent disks are durable and replicated. Performance varies by disk type and size.

Support actions
  • Inspect attached disks in instance details
  • Check disk I/O and latency metrics
  • Consider resizing or changing disk type for performance
Misconception

Assuming disk performance is identical across types can hide the real source of latency.

Concrete example

A database on a VM shows slow queries. Monitoring shows high disk latency. Attach or migrate to a higher-performance persistent disk and verify reduced I/O wait times.

Key Takeaway

When disk latency appears in monitoring, inspect persistent disk type and size before changing application settings. Disk characteristics often explain performance problems.

screens.title: Managed databases: Cloud SQL, Cloud Spanner, and Firestore
screens.narratorSegment: Google Cloud provides several managed database options that suit different application needs. Cloud S Q L is a fully managed relational service for MySQL, PostgreSQL, and S Q L Server. It handles backups, patching, and replication so support teams spend less time on routine database administration. Cloud Spanner is a globally distributed relational database designed for large, mission-critical applications that require horizontal scaling and strong consistency. Firestore, previously Datastore, is a NoSQL document database suited to mobile and web apps requiring flexible schemas. A practical support distinction is the expected operational patterns: Cloud S Q L focuses on conventional relational workloads where you might check instance size, failover status, and automated backups. Cloud Spanner will surface different scaling metrics and is used when applications need global consistency. Firestore troubleshooting often looks at queries, indexes, and document rules. A common misconception is that all managed databases remove the need for any database understanding; in reality, you still need to know schema constraints, backup behavior, and how to access logs for performance troubleshooting. For support staff, map the application's data model to the right service and learn the Console pages and metrics each service exposes.

keyIdea.text: Cloud SQL for traditional relational workloads, Cloud Spanner for global scale, and Firestore for flexible NoSQL document use cases.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.4 › Managed Databases
Relational, distributed, or document?

Cloud SQL, Cloud Spanner, and Firestore serve different workloads. Support tasks depend on the service's operational model.

Cloud SQL
Managed MySQL/Postgres/SQL Server for typical relational needs. Check backups, failover, and instance size.
Cloud Spanner
Globally distributed relational DB for mission-critical scale and consistency. Monitor regional replication and throughput.
Firestore
Document NoSQL for mobile/web apps with flexible schemas. Troubleshoot query performance and indexes.
Concrete example

A transactional application with complex joins fits Cloud SQL. A global financial ledger that must scale horizontally and remain consistent points to Cloud Spanner. A mobile app storing user profiles and activity logs may use Firestore.

Key Takeaway

Understand the data model and scale needs before choosing a managed database. Each service exposes different metrics and troubleshooting steps.

screens.title: Networking services in GCP
screens.narratorSegment: Networking ties compute and storage together and is central to diagnosing connectivity or latency issues. GCP's Virtual Private Cloud is a global software-defined network where you create subnets, assign IP ranges, and configure firewall rules. Cloud Load Balancing distributes incoming traffic across instances to improve availability and scale. Cloud DNS provides name resolution and Cloud CDN caches content closer to users for lower latency. Secure hybrid connections to on-premises networks use Cloud VPN or Interconnect. For support teams, typical tasks include checking VPC subnet ranges, verifying firewall rules, and confirming that a load balancer forwards traffic to healthy backends. A concrete diagnostic example: if users cannot reach a service, check DNS resolution, then load balancer health checks and firewall rules, and finally subnet routing. A common misconception is that firewall rules always block traffic by default; in some setups, overly permissive rules hide misconfigurations. Being systematic — DNS, load balancer, firewall, subnet — yields faster isolation of networking problems. Learn the Console pages that show VPC topology, firewall rule lists, and load balancer backends so you can perform each check quickly.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.4 › Networking
Core networking building blocks

VPC networks, load balancers, DNS, CDN, and secure connections are the core services that shape traffic flow and performance in GCP.

VPC Network
Define IP ranges, subnets, and firewall rules to control internal and external traffic.
Load Balancing
Distribute requests across instances and check backend health for availability.
Cloud DNS & CDN
DNS maps names to IPs; CDN caches content to reduce latency closer to users.
VPN / Interconnect
Secure connections for hybrid clouds and private networking to on-premises systems.
Diagnostic sequence
  1. Confirm DNS resolution for the service domain.
  2. Check load balancer health checks and backend statuses.
  3. Review firewall rules and subnet routing for blocked traffic.
  4. Validate VPN or Interconnect links if hybrid connectivity is used.
Key Takeaway

Use a repeatable diagnostic order — DNS, load balancer, firewall, routing — to find connectivity issues quickly and consistently.

screens.title: How IT support interacts with GCP

The three main interfaces are the Cloud Console for a graphical overview, the gcloud command-line tool for reproducible CLI actions, and gsutil for object storage operations. Support tasks include monitoring resource usage, troubleshooting connectivity, and managing access via Identity and Access Management. Monitoring involves checking C P U, disk, and network metrics and looking at logs for error patterns. Cost optimization is a recurring support responsibility: verify whether expensive machine types or storage classes are necessary, and recommend changes based on observed usage. A common misconception is that permissions issues are always caused by IAM misconfiguration; sometimes the root cause is a network or service-level setting. Practice a concise process: reproduce the problem, collect evidence, test a corrective action in a safe environment, and document the steps. This workflow keeps support responses efficient and auditable. content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.4 › Support Workflow
Interfaces and routine checks

Use the Console for visual checks, gcloud for repeatable actions, and gsutil for storage operations. IAM governs who can do what.

1. Reproduce
Try to reproduce the issue in Console or CLI to confirm symptoms before changing anything.
2. Collect evidence
Gather monitoring graphs, logs, and configuration snapshots to build an initial hypothesis.
3. Test fixes safely
Apply configuration changes in a safe environment or use a rollback plan when modifying production resources.
Concrete scenario

User reports slow website. Reproduce by requesting the site, gather CPU, disk, and load balancer metrics, check firewall rules, and then test scaling or disk changes in a staging environment before applying to production.

Common mistake

Changing production configuration without evidence can create larger incidents. Always collect metrics and have a rollback plan.

Key Takeaway

A reproducible, evidence-led process protects users and helps you resolve incidents with confidence and traceability.

screens.title: Simulated Console exploration and diagnosis
screens.narratorSegment: This guided exercise trains you to navigate the Cloud Console mentally and to conduct a quick diagnostic. Imagine you open the Console and need to find Compute Engine: you would open the main menu, select Compute, and then choose Compute Engine. For Cloud Storage, open the main menu, select Storage, and then Cloud Storage to view buckets. As a support action, open a Compute Engine instance's details page and look for the Monitoring tab to check C P U, disk, and network charts. For the slow website scenario, the first place to look is the instance's Monitoring tab to see whether C P U or disk input and output is high. If metrics are normal, check the load balancer health checks and firewall rules. Practice verbalizing each step as you navigate: this builds a checklist you can follow quickly during real incidents. A common mistake is jumping to change instance size before confirming that current metrics justify it. Finish by documenting your findings: which metric was abnormal, what you changed, and what you recommend next. This simulated exploration prepares you to act confidently in the Console and to describe what you did to other teams.

Module 05 › Chapter 5.4 › Simulated Console
Simulated walkthrough

Verbally practice finding Compute Engine and Cloud Storage in the Console, opening an instance page, and reading monitoring charts for initial diagnosis.

Steps to practice
  1. Open Console menu → Compute → Compute Engine.
  2. Select an instance and view the Monitoring tab for CPU, disk, and network.

Concrete example

For a slow website, check instance CPU and disk I/O first. If disk latency is high, investigate the persistent disk type before resizing the VM.

Common mistake

Rushing to scale compute without evidence often increases cost without solving the root cause.

Key Takeaway

A short, repeatable Console checklist saves time and yields reliable evidence for support decisions.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we move from cloud fundamentals to concrete services you will encounter on the job. You will meet the major cloud providers and then focus on Google Cloud Platform, exploring the compute, storage, and networking services that support applications at scale. We'll show actual command examples you can use in a terminal and discuss when to use each service. For an IT support specialist, the goal is practical familiarity: recognize service names, map them to common tasks like provisioning a virtual machine, choosing appropriate storage based on access patterns, and diagnosing connectivity issues. You will also learn how support workflows use the Cloud Console, the gcloud command-line tool, and simple monitoring checks. By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain why Compute Engine differs from App Engine, select an appropriate Cloud Storage class for archival data, and identify the first places to look when a hosted VM becomes slow. Think of this chapter as a short tour that gives you actionable vocabulary and examples you can use when supporting cloud-hosted systems. What service would you check first when a website is slow?

These learning objectives define the practical skills you'll build in this chapter. First, you will be able to identify the major cloud providers and name the core services each offers; this matters because support conversations often start by naming the provider and service involved. Second, you will explore compute services in Google Cloud — from virtual machines to serverless functions — and learn when a VM is the right choice versus App Engine or Cloud Functions. Third, you will understand storage options such as object storage, block storage, and managed databases, and how to pick a storage class for cost and access patterns. Finally, you will learn the networking building blocks used to connect resources and secure traffic, including VPCs, load balancing, and VPN. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual cue so you can recall which tool fits which task, and the verified competency milestone shows how to demonstrate that skill in a support scenario.

This second objectives slide focuses on the hands-on tasks you will practice. You will learn how to use the Cloud Console to find service pages and read monitoring metrics, and how to run simple gcloud and gsutil commands to create a VM and upload objects. You'll practice selecting appropriate storage classes in Cloud Storage and attaching persistent disks to VMs for boot and high-performance input and output. You will also learn the basic networking checks: review VPC subnet settings, firewall rules, and the Cloud Load Balancing configuration for traffic distribution. For each objective there is a short two-sentence verification step to show mastery. For example, demonstrating the ability to create a VM using gcloud and then locating its monitoring graphs in the Console proves both CLI and Console fluency. These milestones are chosen because support tasks often require fast diagnosis with the Console and repeatable actions via the CLI.

Many organizations rely on one of three dominant cloud providers: Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud Platform. Knowing at least one platform deeply gives you a working vocabulary and enables you to support systems effectively. This lesson focuses on Google Cloud Platform as our example set because it exposes clear service names and has both CLI and Console tools that match common support tasks. For support staff the important idea is not memorizing every product but mapping real incidents to the right service family — for instance, identifying that a VM performance problem likely involves Compute Engine and persistent disks, whereas a slow web request served by a managed platform might point to App Engine or Cloud Functions. A common misconception is that all cloud vendors are interchangeable; while they provide similar categories, each has different names, default behaviors, and tooling which affect how you diagnose issues. For example, support steps you take in the Console or via the CLI will look different across providers. Practice by picking one provider to reach competency: learn its Console layout, its CLI commands for common tasks, and the names of services you will encounter. That focused fluency makes troubleshooting faster and more accurate.

Compute Engine provides virtual machines you control much like physical servers. In practice, you will create instances with a chosen machine type, operating system image, and boot disk. The important support skills are knowing how to provision a basic VM from the CLI, verify it appears in the Console, and read the instance's monitoring charts for C P U, disk input and output, and network. A concrete example command appears in the lesson content: using a gcloud compute instances create command to spin up a Debian VM in a named zone. After creating a VM, check its monitoring tab in the Console for C P U spikes, memory pressure, and disk latency. A common misconception is that VMs always need manual scaling; rather, you can provision autoscaling groups or use load balancing to distribute load. For diagnosis, start with simple metrics and then inspect persistent disk performance if disk input and output is high. As a support professional, practice a sequence: create the VM with the CLI, confirm in the Console, and collect monitoring data to form an initial hypothesis. That pattern gets you to a reproducible, evidence-backed troubleshooting step.

Google Cloud offers managed compute where you don't manage the underlying servers. App Engine is a platform-as-a-service that lets developers deploy web applications without managing OS or scaling details. Cloud Functions is serverless for single-purpose event-driven functions. The practical difference is control versus convenience: App Engine supports web apps with automatic scaling while abstracting server management; Cloud Functions run tiny units of logic in response to events and are ideal for background tasks or lightweight APIs. A concrete example is deploying a small web app: App Engine is appropriate if you need routing, application frameworks, and automatic scaling for web traffic. Cloud Functions works well for processing uploaded files or responding to Pub/Sub messages. A common misconception is that serverless always costs less; costs depend on usage patterns and execution time. For support professionals, the key skill is recognizing the service type from a symptom — if the application entry points are functions and triggered by events, you will check function logs and event triggers; if it's App Engine, you will check version settings, instance class, and request latency. That mapping guides the next diagnostic steps.

Cloud Storage is Google's object storage service for unstructured data such as images, backups, and static website assets. Objects live in named buckets and are accessed by path and permissions. Storage classes — Standard, Nearline, Coldline, and Archive — trade off cost and access frequency: Standard is for frequently accessed objects, Archive is for long-term retention with infrequent access. A practical command you will use as support staff is gsutil cp to upload a file to a bucket; this is useful when verifying backups or moving test artifacts. For example, copying a local file to a bucket simulates a user upload and lets you check permissions and lifecycle rules. A common mistake is placing rarely accessed archival data in a high-cost class; always align storage class with access patterns. As an IT support professional, you will often check bucket permissions, object metadata, and storage class in the Console or with gsutil to confirm whether access errors or cost concerns are caused by misconfigured classes or lifecycle settings. Cloud Storage and object storage concepts means use buckets and storage classes intentionally: align cost and access frequency, and verify with gsutil or the console.. In practical terms, buckets, objects, storage classes, and a gsutil example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Persistent Disk is durable block storage you attach to Compute Engine VMs. Think of it like a virtual hard drive: it serves as a boot disk or data disk and is replicated to provide high availability. For operational support, Persistent Disk matters because disk performance can be a limiting factor for application throughput and database responsiveness. When diagnosing a slow VM, check whether the disk is a standard persistent disk or a higher-performance SSD-backed option, and look at disk input and output metrics in Monitoring. Another support scenario is replacing a boot disk or expanding disk size — these are common tasks you will perform via the Console or CLI. A common misconception is that Persistent Disks are automatically the same performance across machine types; performance characteristics depend on disk type and size. As a support professional, learn to identify attached disks in the instance details, examine their IOPS and throughput, and consider moving critical workloads to higher-performance disk types when justified by measured bottlenecks. Persistent Disk and block storage means persistent disk is the primary block storage for vms; disk type and size affect i/o performance and support decisions.. In practical terms, durable block storage attached to vms and its support implications. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Google Cloud provides several managed database options that suit different application needs. Cloud S Q L is a fully managed relational service for MySQL, PostgreSQL, and S Q L Server. It handles backups, patching, and replication so support teams spend less time on routine database administration. Cloud Spanner is a globally distributed relational database designed for large, mission-critical applications that require horizontal scaling and strong consistency. Firestore, previously Datastore, is a NoSQL document database suited to mobile and web apps requiring flexible schemas. A practical support distinction is the expected operational patterns: Cloud S Q L focuses on conventional relational workloads where you might check instance size, failover status, and automated backups. Cloud Spanner will surface different scaling metrics and is used when applications need global consistency. Firestore troubleshooting often looks at queries, indexes, and document rules. A common misconception is that all managed databases remove the need for any database understanding; in reality, you still need to know schema constraints, backup behavior, and how to access logs for performance troubleshooting. For support staff, map the application's data model to the right service and learn the Console pages and metrics each service exposes.

Networking ties compute and storage together and is central to diagnosing connectivity or latency issues. GCP's Virtual Private Cloud is a global software-defined network where you create subnets, assign IP ranges, and configure firewall rules. Cloud Load Balancing distributes incoming traffic across instances to improve availability and scale. Cloud DNS provides name resolution and Cloud CDN caches content closer to users for lower latency. Secure hybrid connections to on-premises networks use Cloud VPN or Interconnect. For support teams, typical tasks include checking VPC subnet ranges, verifying firewall rules, and confirming that a load balancer forwards traffic to healthy backends. A common misconception is that firewall rules always block traffic by default; in some setups, overly permissive rules hide misconfigurations. Being systematic — DNS, load balancer, firewall, subnet — yields faster isolation of networking problems. Learn the Console pages that show VPC topology, firewall rule lists, and load balancer backends so you can perform each check quickly.
